question: Q2
title: Prediction-powered inference
authors: Angelopoulos AN, Bates S, Fannjiang C, Jordan MI, Zrnic T
read_level: full text (targeted passages: setup, linear regression, finite-population appendix)
setting: i.i.d. or finite population with simple random labelling; means, quantiles, GLM and linear-regression coefficients; asymptotic CLT-based intervals.
finding: The estimand is defined from the joint (X,Y) law or, in the finite-population appendix, as the minimiser of the population loss over all N fixed (X,Y) pairs. For linear regression, X is both the regressor in the estimand and the input to the predictor f(X); nothing restricts f from using the regressor. Validity requires only that f is independent of the observed (labelled and unlabelled) data, e.g. trained elsewhere. The finite-population version assumes labels on a uniform random subset of size n. Coverage results are asymptotic (lim inf as n,N grow), not finite-sample, and the setting is not a cluster design.

question: Q2
title: PPI++: Efficient prediction-powered inference
authors: Angelopoulos AN, Duchi JC, Zrnic T
setting: i.i.d. labelled/unlabelled samples; binary Z and Y; asymptotic normality.
finding: Power-tuned PPI (lambda) never does worse than classical inference asymptotically. Appendix C treats a group-defined estimand, the odds ratio between Z=1 and Z=0, where the indicator Z is observed on all labelled and unlabelled units while f(X) imputes Y. Inference conditions on all Z indicators, so each group gets its own rectification. This is a working PPI template for a domain-contrast estimand whose domain variable is fully observed. Guarantees are asymptotic.

question: Q2
title: Cross-prediction-powered inference
authors: Zrnic T, Candès EJ
setting: i.i.d.; asymptotic intervals; satellite/remote-sensing examples per abstract.
finding: When no external pretrained model exists, the predictor is trained on the labelled data by K-fold cross-fitting, and each label is debiased with an out-of-fold prediction. This keeps validity when the predictor is fitted on the same labelled sample. The abstract does not discuss estimands defined through predictor inputs.

question: Q2
title: Stratified Prediction-Powered Inference for Hybrid Language Model Evaluation
authors: Fisch A, Maynez J, Hofer RA, Dhingra B, Globerson A, Cohen WW
venue: arXiv preprint (cited as NeurIPS 37, 2024 by later papers)
setting: Stratified sampling of labelled units within each stratum; LLM evaluation datasets; asymptotic.
finding: Strata are any partition of the input space X into K sets fixed in advance, so they may be functions of the same inputs the autorater/predictor sees. Strata are used as an estimation device (stratified sampling, per-stratum lambda), while the estimand stays the population M-estimand. Validity holds without assumptions on the predictor. Results are asymptotic (weighted M-estimator CLT). The paper does not treat strata as defining the estimand.

question: Q2,Q3
title: Prediction-Powered Inference with Imputed Covariates and Nonuniform Sampling
authors: Kluger DM, Lu K, Zrnic T, Wang S, Bates S
read_level: full text (targeted: abstract, problem setup, error-in-covariate case, cluster bootstrap appendix)
setting: Remote-sensing housing/tree-cover data (ridge regression on 8,912 image features for the proxies); clustered experiment with 0.5 degree grid cells; asymptotic bootstrap validity.
finding: Separates error-in-Y, error-in-covariate and error-in-both regressions. In the error-in-covariate case the estimand is the regression on the TRUE covariate Z, measured only on a small complete sample, and an ML proxy Z~ is available for all units. The Predict-Then-Debias estimator with bootstrap CIs is valid under no assumption on model quality and allows weighted, stratified or cluster sampling of the complete sample (cluster bootstrap, Algorithm 5). Key implication: a proxy covariate leaves the true-covariate estimand unchanged only if gold-standard covariate values exist on a sample. Without them, the proxy-defined regression is a different estimand. Guarantees are asymptotic.

question: Q2
title: Cluster-Robust Prediction-Powered Inference
authors: Broska D, Howes M
read_level: full text (targeted: abstract, intro, Appendix A assumptions)
setting: TV news frames clustered by broadcast; superpopulation, asymptotic in number of clusters G.
finding: Extends PPI++ to arbitrary within-cluster dependence with closed-form cluster-robust SEs and a cluster-aware lambda. Allows partially labelled clusters. Earlier cluster-aware PPI (Kluger et al.) needed fully labelled or fully unlabelled clusters. Assumptions are model-based: clusters i.i.d. from a cluster distribution, Bernoulli labelling within clusters with cluster-specific probabilities, and an estimand minimising the expected per-unit loss weighted by cluster size. Validity is asymptotic in the number of clusters. Nothing on estimands defined via predictor features. With standard PPI++ on clustered TV-news data, coverage fell below 60%.

question: Q2
title: PPI is the Difference Estimator: Recognizing the Survey Sampling Roots of Prediction-Powered Inference
authors: Mozer R
setting: Expository/argumentative note; SRS; bias derivation in Appendix A.
finding: Shows the PPI mean estimator equals the Cassel-Särndal-Wretman (1976) difference estimator, and PPI++ corresponds to GREG. Model-assisted estimators are design-consistent whether or not the working model is correct. Named warning (sec. 3.4, eq. 7): for a subgroup contrast estimated with one pooled rectifier, the bias equals the difference in group-specific mean prediction errors, delta0 - delta1. So domain contrasts need domain-specific rectifiers. Also notes that model-assisted estimation treats predictions as fixed census-level auxiliaries, while PPI needs f independent of labels (or cross-PPI). The derivation is under simple random sampling and the paper does not cover cluster designs.

question: Q2
title: Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large Language Models
authors: Egami N, Hinck M, Stewart BM, Wei H
setting: Text-as-data; known labelling probabilities; doubly-robust with K-fold cross-fitting; asymptotic.
finding: Downstream regression of Y on explanatory variables X, with gold-standard labels sampled at known probabilities pi(Q,W,X) (design-based labelling, Assumption 1). The supervised model g-hat(Q,X) explicitly takes the same X used as regressors in the downstream estimand. Pseudo-outcomes g-hat + R/pi (Y - g-hat), with cross-fitting, have the correct conditional mean given (Q,W,X) even when g-hat is misspecified. So feeding the estimand's regressors into the predictor is allowed by design and is even encouraged. Guarantees are consistency and asymptotic coverage, not finite-sample.

question: Q2,Q3
identifier: NBER Working Paper w30861; SSRN abstract_id=4334940
title: Parameter Recovery Using Remotely Sensed Variables
authors: Proctor J, Carleton T, Sum S
read_level: abstract only (SSRN and UC Davis seminar pages; excerpts of PDF via search)
setting: Co-located ground truth and remote-sensing measurements across contiguous US (Rolf et al. data); model-based, empirical.
finding: Using ML/remote-sensing predictions in place of ground truth biases regression coefficients and SEs, more so when the predicted variable is a regressor. Over three quarters of 95% CIs missed the true coefficient. Both classical and structured (non-classical) measurement error contribute. Multiple imputation with a calibration sample is proposed. The estimand throughout is the coefficient on the TRUE variable, and the bias is relative to that. The coefficient on the proxy itself is not studied as a target.

question: Q2,Q3
title: Endogenous post-stratification in surveys: Classifying with a sample-fitted model
authors: Breidt FJ, Opsomer JD
read_level: full text (targeted: abstract, sec. 3 assumptions and Result 1)
setting: Forest-inventory motivation (satellite-image classification); general probability designs; simulations.
finding: Post-strata come from a classification model (GLM) fitted on the survey sample itself (endogenous), which breaks the usual post-stratification assumptions of error-free classification and known post-stratum counts. Result 1 gives design consistency under general unequal-probability designs (N to infinity, fixed number of strata and boundaries). Under a superpopulation model, consistency and asymptotic normality follow, and the estimator is asymptotically equivalent to post-stratification on the true model classes. Key point for this project: the estimand is the population mean of y, and the post-strata are only an estimation device. When a sample-fitted classifier instead DEFINES a domain estimand, the estimand itself becomes sample-dependent, which this paper does not cover. Guarantees are asymptotic.

question: Q2,Q3
title: Model-assisted estimation of domain totals, areas, and densities in two-stage sample survey designs
authors: Andersen H-E, Ståhl G, Cook BD, Morton DC, Finley AO
setting: Forest inventory, lidar in sampling mode, SRS and systematic two-stage simulations.
finding: Two-stage design (PSUs, then SSUs/plots) with lidar auxiliaries. The domain-total estimator sums predicted domain membership q-hat_k times predicted y over all cells, plus a residual expansion over sampled plots. The domain is the field-measured one, and predicted membership enters only the working model. When membership is built into the regression (e.g. biomass zero off forest), q-hat can be dropped. Simulations: all estimators approximately unbiased. Variance estimators were unbiased without post-stratification but increasingly biased with post-stratification at low sampling intensity. This is the closest survey analogue found for two-stage designs where model-derived domain information enters the estimator. Guarantees are simulation-based and design-based approximate.

question: Q2,Q3
identifier: Journal of Official Statistics 20(4):645-669 (2004); secondary via doi:10.1177/0282423X251352293 and arXiv:2606.08289
title: Borrowing strength is not the best technique within a wide class of design-consistent domain estimators (with Estevao & Särndal 1999, Survey Methodology, 'The use of auxiliary information in design-based estimation for domains')
authors: Estevao VM, Särndal C-E
venue: Journal of Official Statistics; Survey Methodology
read_level: secondary (search excerpts and Lehtonen 2025 JOS retrospective; scb.se and statcan PDFs blocked)
setting: Design-based; asymptotic design consistency.
finding: As described by secondary sources: when auxiliary information specifies domain membership and auxiliary values for every population unit, GREG-type domain estimators built at domain level are design-consistent. Putting the auxiliary total at the domain level does better than at a level above the domain. Within design-consistent estimators, borrowing strength from outside the domain is not the best approach. For this project: if image-derived domain membership is known for all units, domain-specific assisting models (one per domain) are the standard design-based choice. Not read directly.

question: Q2
title: Direct domain estimation via regression-tree-assisted estimators in the production of official statistics
authors: Ferreira JP
setting: Uruguayan Continuous Household Survey.
finding: Compares one population-level regression tree, giving uni-weights for any domain, with a domain-specific tree. Both are y-free weighted sums. Extending Estevao and Särndal (1999), the population-level-model estimator tends to behave like Horvitz-Thompson within domains, while domain-specific models can reduce variance substantially. Design-based, asymptotic.

question: Q3
title: On the Variances of Asymptotically Normal Estimators from Complex Surveys
authors: Binder DA
read_level: metadata only (Crossref record) plus secondary descriptions (R survey svyrecvar docs; Skinner LSE manuscript)
setting: General complex/multistage designs; asymptotic.
finding: Per secondary sources: Binder defines the finite-population (census) parameter as the solution of population estimating equations. He estimates it by survey-weighted estimating equations, with variance from the design variance of the summed estimating functions (linearization), and multistage designs are handled recursively. The census parameter is defined from whatever unit values are recorded. A derived regressor therefore yields a different but exactly defined census parameter, with the design-based machinery unchanged provided the regressor is a fixed function of unit data. Guarantees are asymptotic (design CLT). Paper not opened (JSTOR).

question: Q3
title: Estimation in the Presence of Measurement Error
authors: Fuller WA
read_level: metadata only (Crossref) plus secondary (Survey Methodology 2006 and 2005 excerpts)
setting: Survey measurement-error review; model-based error structure.
finding: Secondary excerpts: measurement error can bias estimation of distribution functions and of model/census parameters, and Fuller advocates bias-adjusted estimators. The mechanism, attenuation relative to the true-variable coefficient, is the textbook result (also in a Toronto course note: OLS on an error-prone regressor converges to the true slope times the reliability). The bias is relative to the true-variable parameter and not to the proxy-defined census parameter. Paper not opened.

question: Q3
title: The Role of Sampling Weights When Modeling Survey Data
authors: Pfeffermann D
finding: Not read. Listed because it is the standard reference on descriptive (census) vs model parameters in survey regression, and it is a candidate for proxy retrieval. No finding claimed.

question: Q3
title: Model Assisted Survey Sampling (Chapter 10, Estimation for Domains)
authors: Särndal C-E, Swensson B, Wretman J
finding: Chapter 10 has sections on basic domain estimation (10.3), conditioning on domain sample size (10.4), regression estimators for domains (10.5), a ratio model per domain (10.6), group models (10.7), and the comparison of two domains (10.9). The table of contents does not address derived or misclassified domain membership. Content not read.

question: Q3
title: Sampling: Design and Analysis, 3rd ed.
authors: Lohr SL
finding: Domain estimation appears in the ratio and regression chapter (domain means as ratio estimators), and regression with complex survey data in chapter 11. No content on derived regressors was read.

question: Q3
title: Alternative survey sample designs: Sampling with multiple overlapping frames
authors: Lohr SL
read_level: secondary (search-result excerpts of the full text; PDF host blocked)
setting: Dual/multiple-frame surveys; simulation.
finding: Section 6 treats domain misclassification in multiple-frame surveys. Estimators can show severe bias under misclassification, and post-stratifying to domain totals when there is misclassification causes bias. An adjustment is proposed when misclassification probabilities are known. Here the target is the TRUE domain, so the bias is relative to that.

question: Q3
title: A single frame multiplicity estimator for multiple frame surveys
authors: Mecatti F
setting: Multiple-frame surveys; simulation.
finding: Proposes an unbiased multiplicity estimator that needs only the number of frames a unit belongs to, so it is insensitive to domain misclassification. Simulations compare relative bias under growing misclassification rates. The domains are frame-overlap domains, which is tangential to analytic domains defined by a covariate.

question: Q3
title: Adjusting for Misclassification: A Three-Phase Sampling Approach
authors: Sang H, Lopiano KK, Abreu DA, Lamas AC, Arroway P, et al.
setting: US NASS June Area Survey + ALUS; three-phase design.
finding: Misclassification of farms and non-farms biased the JAS farm count. A follow-on survey that measures the true class (a third phase) gives a design-unbiased estimator extending the Särndal-Swensson two-phase estimator, with an explicit design-unbiased variance estimator. Shows the design-based route for a TRUE-class estimand: a validation phase on a probability subsample.

question: Q3
title: Analysis of categorical data for complex surveys
authors: Skinner CJ
setting: Review.
finding: Describes the finite-population regression coefficient computed from all (y_i, x_i) as the census parameter, citing Binder (1983) for why it is of interest and how to estimate it design-based (pseudo-maximum likelihood). The parameter is defined by the recorded x_i values.

question: Q3
title: Impact of Frequentist and Bayesian Methods on Survey Sampling Practice: A Selective Appraisal
authors: Rao JNK
setting: Review.
finding: Survey-weighted estimating equations give design-consistent estimators of census parameters, which in turn estimate model parameters. Resampling variance estimators give asymptotically valid design-based inference, and the approach extends to multilevel models under multistage designs. Asymptotic.

question: Q3
title: Estimates in subpopulations
authors: Lumley T
setting: Software documentation.
finding: Domain means are ratio estimators, or equivalently regression coefficients on a domain indicator. Subsetting the data and treating the result as a new survey gives correct point estimates but wrong SEs. So a domain mean difference is a ratio-type (not exactly design-unbiased) estimator regardless of how the domain is defined.

question: Q3
title: Fitting Regression Models to Survey Data
authors: Lumley T, Scott A
setting: Review.
finding: Reviews design-based regression for complex surveys (NHANES illustration). The abstract has nothing specific on derived covariates.

question: (b),(c)
title: Econometric Issues in the Analysis of Regressions with Generated Regressors
authors: Adrian Pagan
read_level: secondary (OpenAlex metadata only; content as described by Battaglia et al. arXiv 2402.15585 and Oxley & McAleer doi:10.1111/j.1467-6419.1993.tb00158.x)
setting: Asymptotic, model-based, iid or time series; no cluster treatment in the secondary descriptions.
finding: Classical generated-regressor result as described by secondary sources: when a regressor is estimated in a first stage, second-step standard errors that ignore first-stage sampling error are wrong (variance inflation), but the point estimator is not shifted; the target is the parameter on the variable the first stage estimates. Battaglia et al. contrast this with the ML case, where the problem is a location (bias) shift rather than a variance one.

question: (b),(c)
title: Estimation and Inference in Two-Step Econometric Models
authors: Kevin M. Murphy, Robert H. Topel
setting: Asymptotic, parametric two-step M-estimation; independent observations; no few-cluster theory.
finding: Imputed regressors from an auxiliary model carry sampling error; second-step covariance that ignores it gives biased tests even in large samples. Gives a general correction for asymptotically valid standard errors. The target is the parameter on the latent quantity being imputed (e.g. expectations); only inference, not the point estimand, is corrected.

question: (b),(c)
title: Econometric Issues in Macroeconomic Models with Generated Regressors
authors: Les Oxley, Michael McAleer
setting: Macro time-series survey; asymptotic, model-based.
finding: Review of the generated-regressor literature. Two-step estimation is typically inefficient, sometimes efficient; misspecification and measurement error in generated 'surprise' terms are treated as separate threats to validity.

question: (b)
title: Nonparametric regression with nonparametrically generated covariates
authors: Enno Mammen, Christoph Rothe, Melanie Schienle
setting: Asymptotic, iid; first step consistent for the latent covariate.
finding: Stochastic expansion that isolates the effect of a nonparametric first step on a nonparametric second-step estimator, with rates and asymptotic distributions. The target is the regression on the true (unobserved) covariate, which the first step estimates consistently.

question: (b)
title: Two-Step Estimation and Inference with Possibly Many Included Covariates
authors: Matias D. Cattaneo, Michael Jansson, Xinwei Ma
setting: Asymptotic (k comparable to sqrt n), iid; not clustered.
finding: When the first step uses many covariates, the two-step estimator has a first-order bias that invalidates standard inference. A jackknife bias correction and a bootstrap restore validity. The parameter is defined on the latent first-step quantity.

question: (a),(c)
title: Machine Learning Predictions as Regression Covariates
authors: Christian Fong, Matthew Tyler
setting: Regression with an ML-predicted covariate plus a validation subset; simulations and one text application. Asymptotic per secondary descriptions (Battaglia et al. say validity was shown for m/n -> c > 0).
finding: Covariates that are latent (text sentiment) or uncollected (race) are predicted by ML trained on a labelled subset. Plugging the predictions in makes the regression biased, inconsistent and overconfident. They propose a correction that uses the labelled subset. The target is the coefficient on the true covariate, so the proxy is a threat to validity, not a redefinition.

question: (a),(b),(c)
title: Inference for Regression with Variables Generated by AI or Machine Learning
authors: Laura Battaglia, Timothy Christensen, Stephen Hansen, Szymon Sacher
setting: Asymptotic with drifting DGP sequences; model-based; iid; applications to job postings (remote work), text and topic models.
finding: The target is the coefficient on the latent variable theta_i that the AI/ML output estimates (label imputation, embeddings from dimensionality reduction, indices). Their asymptotics keep measurement error and sampling error comparable. Two-step OLS is then asymptotically normal with the correct variance and consistent SEs, but its centring is shifted: CIs have the correct width and the wrong centre. So the failure is in validity, not just interpretation, and it differs from Pagan's variance problem. Fixes: bias-corrected CIs that need only a small subsample with true theta (it can be external and lack Y), or joint likelihood estimation. For a pre-trained classifier they say the analysis holds conditional on the training sample. They warn that the error may be nonclassical (correlated with the latent variable). No clustering anywhere in the text.

question: (a),(b),(c)
title: Prediction-Powered Inference with Imputed Covariates and Nonuniform Sampling
authors: Dan M. Kluger, Kerri Lu, Tijana Zrnic, Sherrie Wang, Stephen Bates
setting: Asymptotic in N, n; design-based labelling (known inclusion probabilities); iid, weighted, stratified, clustered variants; remote-sensing (MOSAIKS), AlphaFold and census applications.
finding: Predict-Then-Debias for an arbitrary subset of imputed features (including covariates). The target theta is what the estimator would return on an infinitely large complete (ground-truth) sample. The naive estimator on predictions 'targets the wrong parameter', so with a latent target the proxy breaks validity. The PTD estimator converges to theta whatever the proxy quality. Bootstrap CIs are proved valid (asymptotically) with no assumption on the ML model, and the regression estimand stays well defined under misspecification (a projection parameter). Appendix B gives a cluster bootstrap in which whole clusters are labelled with known probability and clusters are resampled. That algorithm comes without separate theory and without any few-cluster guarantee. The authors also say prior work did not address clustered validation samples.

question: outcome vs covariate distinction; (c)
title: Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large Language Models
authors: Naoki Egami, Musashi Hinck, Brandon Stewart, Hanying Wei
setting: Asymptotic (consistency and asymptotic normality); design-based in the labelling step; iid documents.
finding: DSL is about predicted OUTCOMES: surrogate labels Q stand in for a text-based outcome Y, and the explanatory variables X are observed. A doubly robust pseudo-outcome is built from gold labels sampled with known probability. Validity holds even with arbitrarily biased surrogates, given known sampling probabilities bounded away from zero. Naive surrogate use gives bias and undercoverage even at 80-90% accuracy. The target is the regression on the true Y. The main text does not treat a predicted covariate that defines the estimand, and has no clustering.

question: outcome vs covariate distinction
title: Prediction-powered inference
authors: Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates, Clara Fannjiang, Michael I. Jordan, Tijana Zrnic
read_level: abstract only (full text downloaded and keyword-searched only for covariate handling)
setting: Asymptotic (CLT-based) and some finite-sample variants; iid labelled and unlabelled samples.
finding: Valid CIs for means, quantiles and GLM coefficients when a labelled set is supplemented by ML predictions of the LABEL, with no assumption on the predictor. The covariates are observed in both sets; the covariate-shift experiment shifts the observed features, which are never predicted. The target is defined on the true label. Predicted covariates that define the estimand are not addressed.

question: outcome vs covariate distinction
title: Cross-prediction-powered inference
authors: Tijana Zrnic, Emmanuel J. Candès
setting: Asymptotic; iid labelled plus unlabelled data.
finding: Imputes missing LABELS with a model trained by cross-fitting on the labelled set, then debiases. More powerful and stabler than PPI with a split-off training set. The setting is predicted outcomes. I found no Zrnic-Candès paper on predicted covariates; Kluger et al. 2025 (with Zrnic) is the closest work.

question: outcome vs covariate distinction
title: Predictions as Surrogates: Revisiting Surrogate Outcomes in the Age of AI
authors: Wenlong Ji, Lihua Lei, Tijana Zrnic
setting: Asymptotic, semiparametric efficiency; iid.
finding: Links PPI to the surrogate-outcome literature and proposes recalibrated PPI, which learns the optimal imputed loss and always improves on labelled-only estimation. Predictions stand in for OUTCOMES; the target is defined on the true outcome.

question: outcome vs covariate distinction
title: Methods for correcting inference based on outcomes predicted by machine learning
authors: Siruo Wang, Tyler H. McCormick, Jeffrey T. Leek
setting: Model-based correction; train/test/validation split; asymptotic or simulation evidence.
finding: Post-prediction inference (postpi): models the observed-vs-predicted outcome relation on a test split and uses it to correct downstream inference. Covers predicted OUTCOMES only (phenotypes from expression, verbal-autopsy causes).

question: outcome vs covariate distinction
title: Program Evaluation with Remotely Sensed Outcomes
authors: Ashesh Rambachan, Rahul Singh, Davide Viviano
setting: Asymptotic, causal identification; experiments and quasi-experiments.
finding: The remotely sensed variable is modelled as post-outcome (caused by the economic outcome). Combining experimental and observational data nonparametrically identifies the causal effect, with misspecification-robust root-n inference. The proxy is for an OUTCOME, and the target stays on the latent outcome.

question: (a),(c)
title: Machine Learning and Prediction Errors in Causal Inference
authors: Gad Allon, Daniel Chen, Zhenling Jiang, Dennis Zhang
read_level: abstract only (SSRN page via web search)
setting: Asymptotic (consistency); simulations and an empirical dataset; per Battaglia et al., validity is shown for comparable validation and main sample sizes.
finding: Two-stage setup in which ML-predicted variables enter a causal regression. Prediction error can bias results arbitrarily even when the specification is otherwise correct. First-stage accuracy and p-values are poor signals of a correct second stage. Consistent corrections need unbiased training (validation) data. The target is the parameter on the true variable.

question: (a),(c)
title: EnsembleIV: Creating Instrumental Variables from Ensemble Learners for Robust Statistical Inference with ML-Generated Variables
authors: Gordon Burtch, Edward McFowland III, Mochen Yang, Gediminas Adomavicius
setting: Asymptotic IV logic plus simulations; linear and GLM; no few-cluster treatment.
finding: ML-predicted INDEPENDENT variables carry prediction error that acts as measurement error and biases regression estimates. Transformed individual learners from an ensemble serve as instruments to correct it. The target is the coefficient on the true variable.

question: (a),(c)
title: When Predictions Become Regressors: A Split-Sample Correction for Biases in Downstream Inference
authors: Nathan Canen, Ted Enamorado
setting: Asymptotic; simulations; political-science text applications; no cluster theory.
finding: Says explicitly that under classical error the OLS estimand for the coefficient on the prediction equals beta times the reliability ratio: the projection parameter on the proxy differs from the latent-variable parameter. This is the clearest statement in my search that naive plug-in identifies a proxy projection. The authors treat it as bias relative to the latent target. Fix: IV from predictions trained on independent sample splits, assuming errors uncorrelated across measures given the input.

question: (a),(c)
title: Large Language Models: An Applied Econometric Framework
authors: Jens Ludwig, Sendhil Mullainathan, Ashesh Rambachan
venue: NBER Working Paper 33344; Annual Review of Economics
setting: Mostly identification and asymptotic arguments; applications use date and company clustered SEs but give no few-cluster theory.
finding: Defines the target concept V_r = f*(r), where f* is the measurement procedure the researcher would use without cost limits. The estimand is the downstream parameter under f*. Plug-in LLM labels are valid for any research context only if they reproduce f* exactly. Errors that correlate with economic variables bias estimates, so this is a validity problem. They show that changing prompt or model flips the sign and significance of regression coefficients. Fix: a small validation sample measured with f* plus debiasing.

question: (a),(c)
title: Econometric Inference with Machine-Learned Proxies: Partial Identification via Data Combination
authors: Lixiong Li
setting: Asymptotic size control, analytic critical values; iid; no clustering.
finding: Treats the ML proxy as a linking variable between a downstream sample (covariates plus proxy) and a validation sample (proxy plus true target), not as a noisy substitute. This yields sharp identified sets for moment-model parameters defined on the latent variable, via optimal transport. The sets shrink to a point when the proxy is exact, and validity does not depend on proxy accuracy. The upstream ML model is treated as fixed when its training sample is independent of the analysis data.

question: (a),(c)
title: Parameter Recovery Using Remotely Sensed Variables
authors: Jonathan Proctor, Tamma A. Carleton, Sandy Sum
setting: Empirical and simulation (bootstrap over grid cells); one application with state-season clustered SEs; no few-cluster theory.
finding: Across many pairs of satellite-predicted variables, using the prediction as the regressor (error-in-X) or as the outcome (error-in-Y) both bias coefficients. In error-in-X, exaggeration is common, not just attenuation, because the errors are nonclassical: mean reversion and differential error. SEs and coverage are also distorted. Multiple imputation using a small labelled set reduces bias and restores coverage. The target is the ground-truth coefficient.

question: (a),(c)
title: Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies
authors: Dean Knox, Christopher Lucas, Wendy K. Tam Cho
setting: Conceptual and graphical; model-based; no inference theory for few clusters.
finding: Learned proxies carry noise and contamination from other concepts, which biases point estimates and SEs. Causal diagrams relating the concept to the proxy show which conclusions survive. Sign-the-bias reasoning can still support valid tests of the existence and direction of an effect.

question: (a)
title: From Unstructured Data to Demand Counterfactuals: Theory and Practice
authors: Timothy Christensen, Giovanni Compiani
read_level: abstract only (arXiv API; intro snippet via web search)
setting: Structural demand models; asymptotic.
finding: Imperfect proxies from unstructured data bias demand counterfactuals and invalidate inference. The intro frames the issue as model misspecification rather than measurement error, an alternative to the latent-variable framing. It offers SE formulas and proxy-quality diagnostics.

question: (a),(c)
title: Imputation-Powered Inference for Missing Covariates
authors: Junting Duan, Markus Pelger
setting: Asymptotic; panel/finance application; clustering not stated in the abstract.
finding: Imputes missing covariates with any method, corrects the imputation bias and weights imputed values by quality. Gives asymptotically normal, valid inference under general missingness patterns. The target is the parameter on the true covariates.

question: (a),(c)
title: Recent Advances in the Measurement Error Literature
authors: Susanne M. Schennach
setting: Survey; asymptotic, model-based.
finding: Surveys estimation and inference for nonlinear models with mismeasured data, classical and nonclassical. Identification relies on auxiliary information (repeated measurements, indicators, instruments); covers set identification and latent-variable links. In all of it the parameter is defined on the latent true variable, and without auxiliary information it is generally not point identified.

question: (c)
title: Mismeasured Variables in Econometric Analysis: Problems from the Right and Problems from the Left
authors: Jerry A. Hausman
setting: Expository; asymptotic, model-based.
finding: Classical error in a single regressor biases the slope toward zero. Reviews IV difficulties and nonlinear corrections. Error in the outcome (left side) is harmless in linear models but not in binary-choice or duration models.

question: (a),(c) for theta_2-type group indicators
title: Identification and Estimation of Regression Models with Misclassification
authors: Aprajit Mahajan
setting: Nonparametric identification; kernel estimator; large-sample theory; iid.
finding: Misclassification in a binary regressor, possibly correlated with other regressors, leaves the regression function unidentified unless an extra variable is correlated with the true class and unrelated to the misclassification. Relevant to a thresholded proxy group indicator: the group contrast on the proxy differs from the contrast on the true class.

question: (a),(b)
title: Sampling-Based versus Design-Based Uncertainty in Regression Analysis
authors: Alberto Abadie, Susan Athey, Guido W. Imbens, Jeffrey M. Wooldridge
setting: Finite-population, design-based plus sampling-based; asymptotic in n; not few-cluster.
finding: Defines descriptive estimands as functions of the finite population's (Y, X) values, as distinct from causal ones. EHW SEs are conservative under design-based uncertainty, and a finite-population correction exists for descriptive estimands. Characteristics held fixed across repeated samples ('attributes') can sharpen variance estimates. Implication for the project: a label-free, deterministic function of each unit's image is an attribute, so a parameter defined on it is a well-posed finite-population estimand. Generated-regressor issues arise only if the construction itself is random or sample-dependent.

question: (a)
title: Models as Approximations I: Consequences Illustrated with Linear Regression
authors: Andreas Buja, Lawrence Brown, Richard A. Berk, Edward I. George, Emil Pitkin, Mikhail Traskin, Kai Zhang, Linda H. Zhao
setting: Asymptotic; iid; model-robust.
finding: Under misspecification, OLS slopes are statistical functionals (projection parameters) of the joint x-y distribution. The regressor distribution changes the slope, and regressor randomness adds root-n variability, so inference needs sandwich or x-y bootstrap SEs. This is the formal basis for treating a proxy-defined slope as a projection parameter, interpretable for the proxy's distribution.

question: (a)
title: Assumption-lean Inference for Generalised Linear Model Parameters
authors: Stijn Vansteelandt, Oliver Dukes
setting: Asymptotic, semiparametric; iid.
finding: Builds on projection-parameter ideas to define nonparametric main-effect and effect-modification estimands that reduce to GLM parameters when the model is correct and keep a meaning when it is not. Inference uses efficient influence functions with ML nuisances. Relevant to defining a slope on a covariate without trusting a model.

question: (b)
title: Bootstrap-Based Improvements for Inference with Clustered Errors
authors: A. Colin Cameron, Jonah B. Gelbach, Douglas L. Miller
setting: Monte Carlo plus asymptotic-refinement arguments; few clusters.
finding: With 5-30 clusters, cluster-robust Wald tests over-reject. A wild cluster bootstrap-t brings rejection near nominal in Monte Carlo. Regressors are treated as observed; generated regressors are not covered.

question: (b)
title: t-Statistic Based Correlation and Heterogeneity Robust Inference
authors: Rustam Ibragimov, Ulrich K. Müller
setting: Small-q exact (Bakirov-Szekely) for Gaussian inputs; large within-group asymptotics; clustered, panel, spatial data.
finding: Estimate the parameter separately in q >= 2 groups and run a t-test on the q estimates. At 5% or lower the test is conservative if the group estimates are independent, unbiased and Gaussian with possibly unequal variances (finite-sample for exactly Gaussian inputs, asymptotic otherwise). It needs per-group unbiasedness, so a group-level bias from a proxy (a shifted centre) would not be removed.

question: (b)
title: Randomization Tests Under an Approximate Symmetry Assumption
authors: Ivan A. Canay, Joseph P. Romano, Azeem M. Shaikh
setting: Fixed G, within-cluster n -> infinity; asymptotic.
finding: Sign-change randomization tests on cluster-level estimates for a fixed number of large clusters. Size is controlled asymptotically as within-cluster size grows, allowing heterogeneous and dependent clusters. Like Ibragimov-Müller, it presumes cluster estimates centred at the target.

question: (b)
title: Cluster-robust inference: A guide to empirical practice
authors: James G. MacKinnon, Morten Ørregaard Nielsen, Matthew D. Webb
setting: Guide; asymptotic theory plus simulation.
finding: Practice guide to cluster-robust inference (few or unbalanced clusters, wild cluster bootstrap, jackknife). Regressors are taken as observed; the abstract says nothing about generated regressors.

question: (b)
title: Wild Bootstrap for Instrumental Variables Regressions with Weak and Few Clusters
authors: Wenjie Wang, Yichong Zhang
setting: Fixed G, within-cluster n -> infinity; asymptotic.
finding: The nearest few-cluster result for a two-stage estimator: with a fixed number of large clusters, the wild bootstrap Wald test for IV controls size up to a small error if identification is strong in at least one cluster. The first stage is estimated on the same clustered data. It is not about ML-generated covariates, but it is a template for few-cluster inference when a first-stage fit enters the second stage.
